config.title: Palindrome Linked List

intro.title: Palindrome Linked List
intro.body: In this lesson, you will build a function that checks if a singly linked list is a palindrome, meaning it reads the same forwards and backwards. You will learn how to traverse a linked list using pointers and compare values efficiently. The main technologies involved are JavaScript's basic data structures and control flow constructs like loops and conditionals. This exercise will help you understand fundamental linked list operations and algorithm design for beginners.
intro.usecase: The palindrome linked list pattern is essential in data validation systems where sequences must be checked for symmetry, such as verifying serial numbers, license keys, or transaction IDs that follow mirroring rules. In user interfaces, this algorithm can power features like undo/redo history validation in text editors or code editors, ensuring operation sequences maintain consistency. It's also used in network packet analysis tools to detect symmetrical data corruption patterns, and in gaming applications to validate symmetrical move sequences in puzzle or strategy games.

objectives: Construct a linked list data structure with nodes containing character values
Implement a function to traverse the linked list and collect node values
Apply a two-pointer technique to compare values from both ends of the list
Manipulate pointers to reverse the second half of the linked list for comparison
Initialize and control multiple pointer variables during list traversal
Integrate helper functions for list reversal and midpoint finding into the main solution
Configure the algorithm to handle both even and odd-length linked lists

content.body: A palindrome reads the same forwards and backwards, like 'racecar'. But how can we check if a linked list is a palindrome when we can't jump to positions? Let's learn how to traverse nodes one by one to solve this.
content.title: Introduction

content.body:
• Apply the pointer mental model to traverse a linked list.
• Implement a method to find the middle of a linked list.
• Explain why we can't use direct indexing with linked lists.
• Reverse the second half of a list to compare with the first half.
• Combine these steps to check for a palindrome.
content.title: What you'll learn

content.body: Imagine you have a linked list: 1 → 2 → 3 → 2 → 1. How would you check if it's a palindrome without knowing the length or using indices? Think about how you'd walk through it node by node.
content.title: Try it
content.visualMetaphor: Show node-to-node traversal; one step at a time along the chain.

content.body: You likely thought about comparing the first and last nodes, then moving inward. But with a linked list, you can't directly access the last node—you have to walk all the way from the head. That's the core challenge.
content.title: What you did

content.body: If the list has 1000 nodes, walking to the end for every comparison becomes extremely inefficient. We need a smarter way that only traverses the list once or twice.
content.title: Why it gets hard

content.body: Add a pointer mental model first: we can only move to next (or prev); we cannot jump by index. We'll use two pointers—one slow and one fast—to find the middle in one pass. Then we can reverse the second half and compare it to the first half, all by walking node-to-node.
content.title: Key idea
content.visualMetaphor: Walk node by node; no direct indexing.

content.body:
1. Use slow and fast pointers to find the middle node.
2. Reverse the second half of the list starting from the middle.
3. Compare the first half with the reversed second half by walking both pointers.
4. If all values match, it's a palindrome. This avoids needing indices or multiple full traversals.
content.title: The approach

content.body:
1. Initialize slow and fast pointers at the head.
2. Move slow one step, fast two steps until fast reaches the end—slow will be at the middle.
3. Reverse the list from slow onward.
4. Compare the original head with the reversed head, moving both pointers one step at a time.
5. If all values match, return true; otherwise, false.
content.title: Steps

steps.title: Set up the function
steps.instruction: Create a function called isPalindrome that takes a head parameter (the first node of the linked list). Return true or false.
steps.hint: Start with the function signature and a placeholder return.
steps.expectedOutcome: Function isPalindrome defined with head parameter.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've set up the function structure.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure the function is named isPalindrome and takes head.
steps.feedbackWrong: Let's start with: function isPalindrome(head) { return false; }

steps.title: Initialize pointers
steps.instruction: Inside the function, create two pointers: slow and fast, both starting at head. We'll use these to find the middle.
steps.expectedOutcome: slow and fast variables initialized to head.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Perfect! Pointers are ready to traverse.
steps.feedbackPartial: Almost. Declare both slow and fast and set them to head.
steps.feedbackWrong: Try: let slow = head; let fast = head;

steps.title: Find the middle
steps.instruction: Use a while loop to move slow one step and fast two steps until fast reaches the end (fast is null or fast.next is null). This positions slow at the middle.
steps.hint: while (fast && fast.next) { slow = slow.next; fast = fast.next.next; }
steps.expectedOutcome: Loop that advances slow and fast correctly.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Excellent! You've found the middle node.
steps.feedbackPartial: Check the loop condition and increments.
steps.feedbackWrong: Use: while (fast && fast.next) { slow = slow.next; fast = fast.next.next; }

steps.title: Reverse the second half
steps.instruction: Now reverse the linked list starting from slow (the middle). Create a prev variable initialized to null, and reverse the nodes by adjusting next pointers.
steps.hint: let prev = null; while (slow) { let next = slow.next; slow.next = prev; prev = slow; slow = next; }
steps.expectedOutcome: Second half reversed, with prev as the new head of reversed half.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Well done! The second half is now reversed.
steps.feedbackPartial: Remember to update prev and slow correctly in the loop.
steps.feedbackWrong: Try: let prev = null; while (slow) { let next = slow.next; slow.next = prev; prev = slow; slow = next; }

steps.title: Compare both halves
steps.instruction: With the second half reversed, compare the first half (starting at head) with the reversed half (starting at prev). Walk both pointers one step at a time until the reversed half ends.
steps.hint: while (prev) { if (head.val !== prev.val) return false; head = head.next; prev = prev.next; }
steps.expectedOutcome: Loop that compares values and returns false if mismatch.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You're comparing node by node.
steps.feedbackPartial: Make sure to check values and move both pointers.
steps.feedbackWrong: Add: while (prev) { if (head.val !== prev.val) return false; head = head.next; prev = prev.next; }

steps.title: Return the result
steps.instruction: If the loop completes without returning false, all values matched, so return true.
steps.hint: After the comparison loop, simply return true.
steps.expectedOutcome: Function returns true at the end.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Perfect! Your function now correctly identifies palindromes.
steps.feedbackPartial: Don't forget to return true after the loop.
steps.feedbackWrong: Add: return true; at the end of the function.

content.body: You've implemented an efficient palindrome check for linked lists! Remember: we can't use indices, so we walk node-by-node with pointers. The slow/fast technique finds the middle in one pass, and reversing the second half lets us compare without extra space. Keep practicing this pointer mental model—it's essential for linked list lessons.
